questions.q: Project $b = (1.5, 2.5)$ onto the line through $a = (3, 1)$. What is the projection $p$?
questions.explain: $a\cdot b = 4.5 + 2.5 = 7$, $a\cdot a = 10$, so $p = 0.7\,a = (2.1, 0.7)$. Forgetting to divide by $a\cdot a$ gives $(21, 7)$; the scalar 0.7 alone is the coefficient, not the vector.

questions.q: $P$ is the orthogonal projection matrix onto a plane. Which pair of properties must it satisfy?
questions.explain: Projecting twice changes nothing ($P^2 = P$), and an orthogonal (not oblique) projection is symmetric. Its eigenvalues are only 0 and 1, so a projection onto a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is not invertible ($\det P = 0$).

questions.q: In least squares $\hat y = X\theta$ with $X = [\mathbf 1\; x]$, why do the residuals $r = y - \hat y$ sum to zero?
options: Because the noise has mean zero
Because $\hat y$ is the projection of $y$ onto the column space of $X$, so $r \perp$ every column, including $\mathbf 1$: $\mathbf 1^\top r = 0$
Because the slope is always positive
They only sum to zero when $n = 3$
questions.explain: The normal equations $X^\top r = 0$ say the residual is orthogonal to each column. The column of ones gives $\sum r_i = 0$ and the $x$ column gives $\sum x_i r_i = 0$ — exactly, for any data, not just on average.

questions.q: The columns of $A$ are dependent ($a_2 = 2a_1$). What happens to $P = A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$?
options: $A^\top A$ is singular so the inverse does not exist; use the pseudo-inverse $P = AA^{+}$, which projects onto the line the columns actually span
The projection of every $b$ is $b$ itself
questions.explain: Dependent columns make $A^\top A$ singular. The column space is still well defined (here a line), and $AA^{+}$ is the orthogonal projection onto it; Gram–Schmidt likewise skips the redundant column.
